name: Which changes distinguish the class design and C++ class models from the earlier conceptual model in the Person example? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: The class design model introduces implementation-oriented details such as visibility, accessor operations, and an explicit mother reference.

answers.body: The C++ class model specializes types and references, for example int, double, and Person*.

answers.comment: L4, slide 2: Those details appear later; the conceptual model describes domain information and the mother relationship.

answers.body: Refinement toward implementation requires removing all behavior from the model.
answers.comment: L4, slide 2: The later models retain getAge() and add further operations.

name: Which similarities and differences between an ER diagram and an OO class diagram are emphasized in this lecture? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Both can show attributes and relationships with multiplicities.
answers.comment: L4, slides 4-6: These similarities explain why the models can look alike.

answers.body: An ER model uses primary keys for identity, whereas an OO object has reference identity by default.
answers.comment: L4, slides 4-6: The lecture contrasts primary keys with the object address; slide 20 notes that identity can be changed.

answers.body: The OO paradigm itself provides relational queries that automatically find all instances of a class in memory.
answers.comment: L4, slides 4-6: The lecture warns that relational algebra is absent from the OO paradigm; access paths must be designed.

answers.body: Methods are part of OO class modeling but absent from the ER models compared here.
answers.comment: L4, slides 4-6: Behavior is a key distinction from the ER model.

name: A conceptual class diagram has a many-to-many Company-Person employment association. What follows for its OO implementation? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Several decompositions can realize it, with different efficiency and maintainability properties.
answers.comment: L4, slides 6 and 14: The examples show several implementations of the same conceptual association.

answers.body: The implementation must use exactly the associative-entity solution used to resolve M:N relationships in the relational example.
answers.comment: L4, slides 6 and 14: OO allows direct references, managers, maps, helper objects, and combinations.

answers.body: The best decomposition depends on the requirements and expected context.
answers.comment: L4, slides 6 and 14: The summary requires choosing a solution for a concrete context.

answers.body: The solution with the most structures and classes is necessarily the best.
answers.comment: L4, slides 6 and 14: The lecture warns that both overly simple and overengineered designs can be unsuitable.

name: Company stores its employees in an array; Person has no link to its companies. JobsMngr stores all companies in a list. Which statements about this decomposition are correct?

answers.body: JobsMngr gives clients an access path to registered Company instances.
answers.comment: L4, slides 7-9: A publicly accessible manager mediates access; OO has no automatic scan for all Company instances.

answers.body: getCompanies(person) can scan the companies and test whether each employee list contains the person.
answers.comment: L4, slides 7-9: The slide explicitly implements the reverse query using a loop and company.contains(person).

answers.body: The shown reverse query takes constant time because the association is conceptually bidirectional.
answers.comment: L4, slides 7-9: A conceptual M:N association does not create a reverse index in this one-way implementation.

answers.body: The reverse query may be acceptable with few companies, despite scanning both company and employee lists.
answers.comment: L4, slides 7-9: The lecture accepts the less efficient decomposition for a small expected population; the nested search depends on both list sizes.

name: Company stores employees and Person stores companies, so the employment relationship is represented in both directions. What tradeoffs does the lecture identify?

answers.body: Responsibilities are distributed clearly across the participating classes.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10: Each side provides access to its related objects.

answers.body: Updates must keep both sides consistent, adding synchronization and memory-management concerns.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10: The lecture identifies consistency checking and memory management as costs, especially without garbage collection.

answers.body: Garbage collection automatically guarantees that both collections always agree about employment.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10: Reclaiming memory does not maintain the semantic consistency of two relationship collections.

answers.body: A bidirectional association makes all consistency checks unnecessary.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10: Maintaining the two representations is the main drawback highlighted.

name: JobsMngr instead stores Company-to-Person and Person-to-Company maps. Which assessment matches the lecture?

answers.body: The maps support access in both directions and localize relationship consistency management in JobsMngr.
answers.comment: L4, slide 11: Efficiency and centralized consistency checking are the stated benefits.

answers.body: The manager risks becoming a large God object with too much responsibility.
answers.comment: L4, slide 11: The slide names this as a disadvantage.

answers.body: A salary for each employment naturally belongs to Person alone, even if that person works for several companies.
answers.comment: L4, slide 11: Salary belongs to a concrete company-person relationship; the slide asks where to store it in this map-only model.

answers.body: The two maps remove the need to keep the relationship representations synchronized.
answers.comment: L4, slide 11: They localize consistency work rather than eliminate it.

name: Why introduce a Job object linking one Company and one Person, and what changes when JobsMngr indexes Job sets by company and person?

answers.body: Job can store salary for the particular company-person pair.
answers.comment: L4, slides 12-13: The helper object holds the two references and relationship-specific data.

answers.body: Maps from Company and Person to sets of Job objects improve access but add complexity and consistency work.
answers.comment: L4, slides 12-13: The combined solution gains efficient lookup while potentially reducing maintainability.

answers.body: Indexing jobs is always preferable, regardless of workload or the number of jobs.
answers.comment: L4, slides 12-13: The lecture explicitly says the indexed solution is unnecessarily complicated in many situations.

name: A breeding application and a veterinary application both model cats. Which conclusions about abstraction match the lecture? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: The same real-world cat can be classified and modeled differently depending on the application domain.

answers.body: One generic Cat class containing both domains is automatically more maintainable because it is reusable everywhere.

answers.comment: L4, slides 16-19: The classification quiz demonstrates that several correct abstractions are possible.

answers.body: The lecture contrasts tightly connected classes with components connected through loose contracts when discussing reuse.

name: Which statements about objects and classes match the OO fundamentals summarized in this lecture?

answers.body: Objects are runtime entities that store data behind public operations; classes provide a static design-time view.
answers.comment: L4, slide 20: The slide distinguishes runtime objects from their design-time class descriptions.

answers.body: Concrete field values define object state, and current state can affect method behavior.
answers.comment: L4, slide 20: State is the data; methods define behavior that can depend on that data.

answers.body: Two objects with equal field values must have the same identity.
answers.comment: L4, slide 20: Identity is based on the object address by default, rather than equality of all field values.

answers.body: A class must be a runtime instance and cannot describe the structure of many objects.
answers.comment: L4, slide 20: A class is the static view shared by its objects.

answers.body: Only the class name; changing its behavior or relationships cannot affect its abstraction.
answers.comment: L4, slide 21: Attributes, methods, and surrounding context all influence what the class represents.

name: Which statements apply the single-responsibility principle to the employment examples?

name: ResourceAllocator has a switch over TIME_SLOT and SPACE_SLOT. Which refactoring best follows the open-closed principle when further resource kinds will be added?

name: ClassB inherits ClassA and overrides print() to print B; ClassA.print() prints A. With dynamic dispatch, ClassA object = new ClassB(); object.print(); is executed. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: The call prints B because the runtime object provides ClassB's implementation.

answers.comment: L4, slides 29-30: The lecture uses addition as another illustration of a shared operation with different behavior.

name: What does the Liskov substitution principle require of a subtype?

answers.body: It can replace an instance of the supertype without changing the desirable properties on which the client relies.
answers.comment: L4, slide 30: This is the substitutability requirement stated on the slide.

answers.body: It must preserve both relevant method-signature constraints and behavioral conditions.
answers.comment: L4, slide 30: The lecture groups Liskov's constraints into these two categories.

answers.body: It must implement every method with exactly the same internal code as the supertype.
answers.comment: L4, slide 30: Different implementations are allowed when they preserve the expected contract.

answers.body: Clients must be rewritten to recognize every subtype before substituting it.
answers.comment: L4, slide 30: Requiring subtype-specific adaptation defeats substitution under the existing supertype expectations.

name: Nest.setOwner accepts Animal. Bird is an Animal, and Animal is a Creature. Considering the lecture's substitutability rule rather than a particular language's overriding syntax, which parameter types may BirdNest.setOwner accept?

answers.body: Animal.

name: Draw and explain a UML design for employment: a Person can work for several Companies, a Company can employ several Persons, and salary is specific to each employment. Queries in both directions are frequent. Show relevant multiplicities, references, query operations, and where consistency is maintained. Compare your design with a simple one-way employee-list solution.
answer: One suitable design introduces Job with salary, one Company reference, and one Person reference. Each Job belongs to exactly one company and one person, while each company and person can participate in zero or more jobs. JobsMngr maintains Map<Company, Set<Job>> and Map<Person, Set<Job>>, offering getJobs(company) and getJobs(person), from which the related persons or companies can be obtained. Keep updates to both indexes together so they describe the same jobs. Job owns the pair-specific data; Company and Person keep their own entity data; the manager owns access and indexing. Compared with Company.employees alone, the indexes avoid scanning all companies and their employee lists for a reverse query, but introduce extra structures and consistency work. A simple list-based design can still be preferable for a small workload; the requirements must justify the indexes. Show general associations or navigable references without inventing lifetime ownership that the requirements do not establish.
keyPoints: Job represents one company-person relationship and stores its salary
Each Job references exactly one Company and one Person; either entity can have zero or more Jobs
The manager provides query paths, optionally using maps to Job sets for the stated frequent queries
Updates preserve consistency of both indexes and distribute entity, relationship, and access responsibilities
Compare lookup efficiency with the simpler one-way design and acknowledge added complexity

name: Draw a UML package/class design that replaces DispatchService's direct dependency on SmsGatewayClient with dependency inversion. Show interface ownership, source dependencies, runtime call direction, and construction. Explain how you would test dispatching and later switch to email.
answer: Put DriverNotifier in the dispatching package, owned by the high-level client and exposing notify(driver, message). DispatchService depends on this interface and receives a notifier through its constructor. Put SmsNotifier in infrastructure and show it realizing DriverNotifier; its technology-specific work can use SmsGatewayClient. This makes infrastructure depend on the dispatching abstraction at source level, while runtime calls still go from DispatchService through the interface to the notifier implementation. A composition root constructs SmsNotifier and passes it to DispatchService; a DI container is an optional way to perform this wiring. For a unit test, supply a fake DriverNotifier and inspect the requested notifications without a live SMS service. To use email, supply an EmailNotifier implementing the same client contract. DIP concerns dependency direction and interface ownership; DI concerns supplying objects. Merely putting an interface in infrastructure would leave dispatching dependent on that lower-level package.
keyPoints: DriverNotifier is owned by dispatching and expresses the client's need
DispatchService uses the interface; SmsNotifier realizes it from infrastructure
Source dependency points toward the high-level abstraction while runtime calls still reach the low-level implementation
An external composition root or DI container constructs and supplies the implementation
Fake and EmailNotifier implementations preserve dispatching code; DIP is distinct from DI

name: Using the Public Transport supplement, sketch two UML designs: (a) a nested city plan whose elements support highlight(), and (b) a daily work schedule whose shift behavior changes between workdays and vacations. Identify pattern roles, relationships, and which runtime links can change. Explain why the context does not need to change its own class.
answer: For (a), use Composite: CityPlanElement declares highlight(); Leaf and Composite inherit that contract; Composite associates with zero or more CityPlanElement children. ConstructionSign and LineNumber are leaves, while CityPlan, Line, and Stop are composites in the supplied example. The common contract lets the design handle a single element and a subtree uniformly; preserve any domain restrictions on allowed children separately. For (b), use State: DailyWorkSchedule is the context and holds one CurrentDay interface; WorkDay and VacationDay realize getShift(lineNo, numDriver). updateToday() replaces the associated state object according to the current day, while the schedule delegates day-specific behavior through the same interface. The context retains its class throughout its lifetime; the associated objects and links vary at runtime. The supplement supplies these pattern examples; they are additional material rather than individual slides in the L4 deck.
keyPoints: Composite has a common CityPlanElement contract and a collection of children of that same type
Identify ConstructionSign/LineNumber as leaves and CityPlan/Line/Stop as composites in the supplied model
State separates the DailyWorkSchedule context from the CurrentDay interface and its WorkDay/VacationDay implementations
updateToday() replaces the associated state object; the context's own class stays the same
source: Public Transport supplement, slide/page 16-17 and 19; L4, slides 22-23 (runtime flexibility of association)
